EDIT-02: Existing = wording already present in the design, companion prompt or museum scene. Draft = new wording proposed for review. Dynamic = a runtime template or a bounded example of AI dialogue. Braces such as {specimen_name} are placeholders.
EDIT-03: This document covers entry, navigation, all eight questions and their reactions, the final choice, optional reflection, every result and alternative introduction, incomplete visits, saving and sharing, settings, errors, museum labels and Abraham’s dialogue. Most interface text remains planned rather than implemented.
EDIT-04: You can rewrite freely. If an answer’s meaning changes, flag it for a scoring review; its hidden scoring is intentionally excluded from this copy document. AI-generated wording cannot be listed exhaustively, so editable templates, fixed fallbacks and voice guidance are included.

Q1-INTRO: It’s a very small fossil, but the label has rather a lot to say. Which part would you open?
q1: This fossil cast has a tiny feature that changes how it is understood. You have time to open one part of the display. Which would you choose?
q1-i: How the curators worked out what kind of animal it was.
q1-i-evidence: Chose the evidence behind the fossil’s identification.
q1-c: Which parts are original fossil, and which were restored.
q1-c-confirm: The original and restored areas are marked.
q1-c-evidence: Wanted to distinguish surviving material from later restoration.
q1-a: A chance to study it without the label, then reveal the explanation.
q1-a-confirm: The explanation is folded away. You can open it whenever you like.
q1-a-evidence: Chose space for a first-hand impression before reading the answer.
q1-r: What different visitors noticed when they first saw it.
q1-r-confirm: The three visitor observations are now beside the cast.
q1-r-evidence: Wanted several perspectives on the same fossil.
Q2-INTRO: There’s a gap just there. We know something belonged in it, but not quite what.
q2: This skeleton is missing one piece. Which version would you rather encounter in the museum?
q2-i: Show two possible reconstructions beside the gap so I can compare them.
q2-i-evidence: Preferred competing explanations to a single reconstruction.
q2-c: Leave the gap visible so I can see exactly what remains.
q2-c-confirm: The gap stays open, with the surviving material marked.
q2-c-evidence: Kept an absence visible rather than filling it in.
q2-a: Add a clearly marked, removable replica so I can picture the whole animal.
q2-a-confirm: The removable replica is in place.
q2-a-evidence: Chose a reversible way to move forward with incomplete information.
q2-r: Let visitors switch between the possible versions themselves.
q2-r-confirm: The display can now switch between its different views.
q2-r-evidence: Made room for different ways of understanding the skeleton.
Q3-INTRO: Most days don’t leave fossils. We could keep one small trace of yours, though.
q3: This trace-fossil wall has one empty archive slot. If you added a small record of an ordinary day, what would you put at its centre?
q3-i: An unanswered question I kept returning to.
q3-i-confirm: Your question card is clipped into the record.
q3-i-evidence: Kept an unresolved question as the day’s central record.
q3-c: A small routine I might otherwise forget.
q3-c-confirm: Your routine sketch is clipped into the record.
q3-c-evidence: Preserved an easily overlooked part of everyday life.
q3-a: A decision that changed how the day went.
q3-a-confirm: Your decision sketch is clipped into the record.
q3-a-evidence: Focused on a moment of making a difference.
q3-r: An exchange with someone that stayed with me.
q3-r-confirm: Your exchange is clipped into the record.
q3-r-evidence: Remembered the day through an interaction.
Q4-INTRO: The second tray wasn’t on my list. It does look interesting, doesn’t it?
q4: A mineral drawer opens to two trays: one familiar sample and one unexpected find. You only have time for one arrangement. What is closest to your instinct?
q4-i: Read a little more about both samples before choosing which to examine.
q4-i-confirm: The extra information card is open.
q4-c: Stay with the familiar sample and give it the closer look I planned.
q4-c-confirm: The original tray stays in view.
q4-c-evidence: Protected an existing intention while leaving a future opening.
q4-a: Switch to the unexpected sample; I can return to the familiar one later.
q4-a-evidence: Accepted an opportunity while treating the original plan as recoverable.
q4-r: Place both trays side by side and compare them with someone.
q4-r-confirm: Both trays are now side by side.
q4-r-evidence: Looked for a shared comparison that kept both options in view.
Q5-INTRO: One meteorite, one bit of funding, and four sensible forms. I’m glad it isn’t my decision.
q5: If you were helping the museum choose one next step for this unfamiliar meteorite, which would you back?
q5-i: A detailed scan: more information, though it may not settle the main question.
q5-i-evidence: Accepted an incomplete answer in exchange for more evidence.
q5-c: Better storage first: protect the meteorite, though the answer will wait.
q5-c-confirm: The storage cradle is in place.
q5-c-evidence: Protected future options before pursuing an immediate answer.
q5-a: A tiny sample test: a clearer answer, but it permanently uses some material.
q5-a-confirm: The sample diagram is open. The display specimen stays intact.
q5-a-evidence: Accepted a stated cost for a more decisive next step.
q5-r: A joint study with another museum: shared expertise, but a slower start.
q5-r-evidence: Chose shared expertise despite a coordination cost.
Q6-INTRO: Same samples, two different labels. Neither one looks obviously wrong to me.
q6: You and another visitor study the same two mineral samples but leave very different notes. What would you want to do next?
q6-i: Compare the particular details each of us noticed.
q6-i-confirm: The detail markers connect the two accounts.
q6-i-evidence: Explored the observations behind different impressions.
q6-c: Keep both accounts intact; neither needs replacing yet.
q6-c-evidence: Preserved separate accounts without forcing resolution.
q6-a: Try a different viewing angle together and see what changes.
q6-a-confirm: A third viewing angle is available.
q6-a-evidence: Used another experience to move beyond the disagreement.
q6-r: Ask why that impression of the samples mattered to them.
q6-r-evidence: Prioritised the personal significance of another perspective.
Q7-INTRO: Here’s the old habitat, and here’s the proposal. They moved nearly everything.
q7: This miniature habitat is being redesigned. The proposal has real benefits, but it will feel different. What would you speak up for first?
q7-i: A clear account of what the habitat change is meant to improve.
q7-i-evidence: Asked for the purpose and evidence behind a change.
q7-c: Keep one feature that makes the habitat feel like itself.
q7-c-confirm: The feature you would keep is highlighted.
q7-c-evidence: Protected a specific source of continuity.
q7-a: Use a trial layout before making the redesign permanent.
q7-a-confirm: The trial layout is in place.
q7-r: Let the keepers and regular visitors help shape the proposal.
q7-r-confirm: The participation markers are on the proposal.
q7-r-evidence: Prioritised participation by the people affected.
Q8-INTRO: The sensible things are packed. There’s just enough room for one interesting thing.

q8-r: A shared camera, so everyone can add what caught their eye.

VISIT-IC-BALANCED-INTRO: You tended to look for the explanation while keeping sight of what was already there.
VISIT-IC-I-LEADING: Understanding came first; keeping the original context helped you get there.
VISIT-IC-C-LEADING: You kept hold of context, and wanted enough understanding to preserve it thoughtfully.
VISIT-IC-STRENGTHS: retaining useful context; checking the basis of an explanation.
VISIT-IC-TENSION: you may keep investigating or preserving something after you have enough to move on.
VISIT-IC-COMPLEMENT: a small, reversible experiment can give your careful thinking somewhere to go.
VISIT-IC-FRICTION: rapid changes without an explanation may be harder to accept than the change itself.
VISIT-IC-CLOSING: What would count as enough information to take the next step?
VISIT-IC-PATTERN: In this visit, understanding and keeping useful context often appeared together. Your specimen is a way of holding those two concerns in view. It doesn’t mean you have to keep every detail or wait for a complete explanation before acting.

VISIT-IA-BALANCED-INTRO: You wanted to understand things by getting a closer look and trying something with what you learned.
VISIT-IA-I-LEADING: You wanted a sound explanation, with room to test it rather than leave it on the label.
VISIT-IA-A-LEADING: You preferred to move things forward, using new information to choose your next move.
VISIT-IA-STRENGTHS: questioning assumptions; turning curiosity into a next step.
VISIT-IA-TENSION: the next question or experiment may pull you away before the current one is settled.
VISIT-IA-COMPLEMENT: someone who records decisions and follows through can help discoveries accumulate.
VISIT-IA-FRICTION: rules that block both explanation and experimentation may frustrate you.
VISIT-IA-CLOSING: Which possibility would you actually stay with long enough to learn from?
VISIT-IA-PATTERN: In this visit, finding out and doing something with the answer often belonged together. The match reflects that connection. It leaves room for the moments when you preferred to pause, preserve something or hear another view.

VISIT-IR-BALANCED-INTRO: You often wanted to understand a thing through the perspectives and connections around it.
VISIT-IR-I-LEADING: You sought a fuller explanation, and other perspectives were part of the evidence.
VISIT-IR-R-LEADING: Understanding other perspectives mattered, even when it complicated your first impression.
VISIT-IR-STRENGTHS: comparing perspectives; making explanations easier to share.
VISIT-IR-TENSION: you may make room for so many interpretations that your own becomes difficult to state.
VISIT-IR-COMPLEMENT: a clear personal position can give the conversation something concrete to work with.
VISIT-IR-FRICTION: being pushed to agree before the different views have been heard.
VISIT-IR-CLOSING: After hearing everyone else, what is your own best reading?

VISIT-CA-BALANCED-INTRO: You wanted room to make a change without losing everything useful underneath it.
VISIT-CA-C-LEADING: Keeping a dependable base mattered; changes felt worthwhile when they could build on it.
VISIT-CA-A-LEADING: You wanted to act, while keeping a way to revise or return.
VISIT-CA-TENSION: you may prefer changes you can control and postpone ones that require a less tidy transition.
VISIT-CA-COMPLEMENT: an outside question can reveal which familiar constraints are still necessary.
VISIT-CA-FRICTION: being asked to choose between total preservation and starting from nothing.
VISIT-CA-CLOSING: Which part really needs to stay, and which part is simply familiar?

VISIT-CR-FRICTION: changes that treat existing commitments as disposable.
VISIT-CR-CLOSING: What are you willing to maintain—and what needs to be shared?

AB-DREAM-NOTE: These lines are optional fictional museum dialogue. Use only for the matching scene or visitor message. The offer of company is a conversation line, not an implemented follow-player action. Do not promise movement unless the game supports it.
VOICE-01: Abraham is a friendly, earnest little hamster who considers the museum a perfectly normal place to work. He notices its peculiarities but rarely recognises their unsettling implications. He speaks simply and casually, takes small practical concerns seriously, and wants visitors to feel welcome. His warmth is sincere; he isn’t secretly teasing the visitor or delivering knowing hints.
VOICE-02: Most replies are one to three short sentences. Use contractions and concrete words. A small “Oh!”, “Hmm” or “Let’s see” can sound spontaneous, but vary the openings. Not every line needs a joke, hesitation or exclamation.
VOICE-03: Refer only to the choices supplied from this visit. Do not infer personality from the route, timing, accessibility settings or decorative inspection. Do not invent a reason the visitor has not supplied.
VOICE-04: Acknowledge one optional clarification. Do not ask a follow-up question or change the selected specimen.
VOICE-05: Keep the supplied specimen name. Write a short introduction, connect three actual choices, name two strengths and one believable tension, suggest a complementary approach, and close with one reflection. Use the authored result outline as the boundary.
VOICE-06: Prefer “Oh, I see”, “Have a look”, “What should I call you?” and simple references to an actual choice. Describe things Abraham can point to: tickets, drawers, labels and specimens. Keep assessment explanations on the result card; do not make every conversation sound like a report.
VOICE-07: Avoid “This proves”, “You always”, “You clearly value”, “According to my analysis” and therapist-like acknowledgements such as “That’s useful to notice”. No baby talk, constant snack jokes, elaborate metaphors or knowing warnings. He must not imply he has sinister knowledge of the visitor.
VOICE-08: Be welcoming from the first meeting, then become more familiar naturally. Abraham’s friendliness does not depend on quiz choices. He can fail to notice that a room feels creepy while noticing that the visitor wants company. If someone is genuinely upset, listen and respond kindly; do not keep making jokes.
VOICE-09: The specimen is a playful comparison. Do not diagnose, imply scientific validation, claim permanent personality knowledge or say the museum collects people.
VOICE-10: Use the authored specimen introduction, real evidence lines, strengths, tension, complement, friction and closing question. Do not leave the visitor with only a specimen name.
VOICE-11: Neutral is the default expression. Curious or delighted may accompany suitable dialogue; worried must not signal that a quiz choice was bad. These directions describe presentation, not words for Abraham to say.
